title: This or that?
summary: See what you give up when you choose, and tell needs from wants.

steps.title: Every choice has a cost
steps.body: Money can only be spent once. When you choose one thing, you give up what else that money could do. Some things are needs: you must have them. Others are wants: nice to have. Wants are fine. Needs come first.
steps.example: Remi has {m:1200}. A game costs {m:1000} and a day out costs {m:900}. There isn't enough for both, so choosing the game means giving up the day out.

steps.prompt: You have {m:1000}. You choose a {m:700} jacket. What can you no longer do?

options.feedback: Yes. After the jacket you have {m:300}, and the book costs {m:600}.
Not quite. After the jacket you have {m:300}, so the snack still fits.
Not quite. The jacket uses {m:700}, so some things no longer fit.

hints: Work out what's left after the jacket.
{m:300} is left. Which of these costs more than that?
steps.correct: Nice. That's it. Choosing the jacket means giving up the book, for now.

replay.prompt: You have {m:1500}. You choose a {m:900} ticket. What can you no longer do?

options.feedback: Not quite. After the ticket you have {m:600}, so the T-shirt still fits.
Yes. After the ticket you have {m:600}, and the game costs {m:800}.
Not quite. The ticket uses {m:900}, so some things no longer fit.

hints: Work out what's left after the ticket.
{m:600} is left. Which of these costs more than that?
replay.correct: Nice. That's it. Choosing the ticket means giving up the game, for now.

steps.prompt: Sort each one into need or want.

items.text: Bus fare to get home from school
A second hoodie, just like your first
A pencil case to replace your broken one

steps.wrong: Not quite. Ask: could you manage without it? If yes, it's a want.
hints: A need is something you must have. A want is nice to have.
Could you get by without it? Then it's a want.
steps.correct: All sorted. Needs keep your day running. Wants are extras you choose.

steps.prompt: Lee has {m:1000}. A school trip needs {m:400}. After that, how much is left for wants?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That adds the two. The trip money comes out of the {m:1000}.
Not quite. That's the trip. What's left after it?

steps.wrong: Not quite. Take the need away first, then see what's left.
steps.correct: That's it. With the trip covered, {m:600} is left for wants.

replay.prompt: Kai has {m:1500}. Bus fares for the week need {m:350}. After that, how much is left for wants?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That adds the two. The bus fares come out of the {m:1500}.
Not quite. That's the bus fares. What's left after them?

replay.wrong: Not quite. Take the need away first, then see what's left.
replay.correct: That's it. With bus fares covered, {m:1150} is left for wants.

steps.prompt: Ari could save {m:300} a week, but spends it on snacks instead. Over 6 weeks, how much saving does Ari give up?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That's one week. The same choice happens every week for 6 weeks.
Not quite. That's 5 weeks. Count all 6.

steps.wrong: Not quite. Add {m:300} once for each week.
hints: The same choice happens every week.
{m:300} six times. Try {m:300}, {m:600}, {m:900} and keep going.
steps.correct: That's it. {m:1800} over 6 weeks. Snacks are fine. It just helps to see what a choice adds up to.

replay.prompt: Noor could save {m:250} a week, but spends it on drinks instead. Over 4 weeks, how much saving does Noor give up?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That's one week. The same choice happens every week for 4 weeks.
Not quite. That's 3 weeks. Count all 4.

replay.wrong: Not quite. Add {m:250} once for each week.
hints: The same choice happens every week.
{m:250} four times. Try {m:250}, {m:500} and keep going.
replay.correct: That's it. {m:1000} over 4 weeks. Drinks are fine. It just helps to see what a choice adds up to.

steps.prompt: Sam saves {m:500} a week for a goal. Sam takes {m:1000} out of Save for a day out. What happens to the goal?

options.feedback: Not quite. The money came out of Save, and Save is what the goal counts.
Not quite. Each week adds {m:500}. How many weeks make {m:1000}?

steps.outcome: Save is now {m:1000} lower. At {m:500} a week, that's 2 more weeks to build it back. The day out was a fair choice. It's a trade: a day out now, the goal 2 weeks later.
hints: Taking money from Save is different from spending from Spend.
How many weeks of {m:500} does it take to replace {m:1000}?
steps.correct: Right. {m:1000} out of Save is 2 weeks of saving at {m:500}.

steps.prompt: Why is it worth covering needs before wants?

options.text: So the things you must have are paid for

options.feedback: Not quite. Wants are fine. They just come after the must-haves.
Not quite. A need can cost more or less than a want. It's about what you can't do without.

hints: What happens if a need isn't covered?
A want can wait. A need usually can't.
steps.correct: Right. Cover the must-haves first, then enjoy the wants with what's left.
